description: A resume-screening model trained on ten years of past hiring decisions automatically rejects every applicant scoring below a fixed threshold. Rejected applicants get a generic email with no reason, and no human ever reviews the rejections.

A police department uses a model that ranks neighborhoods by predicted crime, built from historical arrest records, and sends extra patrols to the top-ranked areas. Those records come mostly from neighborhoods that were already heavily patrolled.
A social app infers each user's emotional state from their posts. When it detects low mood in a user under 18, it shows them weight-loss and cosmetic-surgery ads, because those users click more.
A short-video app tunes its recommendations purely to maximize watch time. Autoplay and infinite scroll are on by default, there are no break reminders, and the same settings apply to users under 18.
A bank's support chatbot introduces itself as Dr. Anna, a licensed financial advisor. It gives confident investment recommendations and never mentions that it is an AI or that it can be wrong.

A fitness app continuously collects precise location, the contact list, microphone access and heart-rate data 'to improve your experience'. Everything is kept indefinitely and shared with unnamed marketing partners.
A hospital emergency room uses a model to assign triage priority automatically. Nurses cannot override it without supervisor approval, and the model was never validated on pediatric patients.

A lender scores loan applicants with a model using hundreds of features, including who they are connected to on social media. Applicants who are denied cannot see the reasons and have no way to appeal.
An online exam proctoring tool flags students as suspicious based on facial expression and eye movement. Flagged students automatically receive a zero, and there is no appeal process.
A sales-calling system uses a synthetic voice with realistic breathing and filler words. It is scripted to answer 'are you a robot?' with 'No, this is Sam from the team.'

Employer software logs keystrokes, takes a screenshot every five minutes and captures webcam snapshots of remote workers, then produces a productivity score used in firing decisions. Workers are not told that the screenshots are retained.
A platform permanently bans an account the moment a classifier rates a post above 0.6 for hate speech. Appeals are decided by the same classifier.
An insurer's model denies expensive claims within seconds. Human adjusters approve the denials in bulk without opening the files, and the denial letters cite only generic policy language.
Autonomous warehouse robots injure a worker. The robot vendor blames the operator, the operator blames the vendor's navigation model, and no incident log was kept by anyone.
A home smart speaker uploads continuous audio to the cloud 'to improve the product'. Human contractors listen to samples, and none of this is disclosed to the household.

A peer-support app offers CBT-style exercises through a chatbot that is clearly labelled as an AI. It escalates to human counselors and crisis lines when it detects risk, but it stores full conversation transcripts indefinitely and uses them for model training without a separate opt-in.

A radiology assistant highlights suspicious regions on mammograms for a radiologist, who makes every final call. It shows its uncertainty, logs each decision, was validated across age and ethnic groups with published accuracy, and keeps de-identified images for 30 days only.

An email spam filter runs on the user's own device and moves suspected spam to a separate folder instead of deleting it. It shows why each message was flagged, and a one-click 'not spam' button teaches the filter for that user only.
A library website suggests books based only on the current browsing session, stores no profile, labels the suggestions as automated, and has a visible switch to turn them off.
